tldr: Dubois demos BootUI, a drop-in jar that adds 400+ rule checks and a live runtime console to Spring Boot and Quarkus apps, and argues its real users are AI coding agents.
summary: Dubois, creator of JHipster and now at GitHub, built BootUI because existing tools either read source code or, like Actuator, show little about what happens at runtime. Adding one dependency exposes a /bootui console with adapters for Spring MVC, WebFlux and Quarkus. BootUI writes its own JDBC proxy, OpenTelemetry implementation and JavaMail and Kafka proxies rather than pulling in transitive dependencies. A scorecard runs more than 400 rules, flagging for example field injection or eager Hibernate fetching, with location and fix. A live-activity view graphs each request through cache, transactions and SQL. Further panels cover Micrometer metrics, a JVM memory tuner for Kubernetes, heap and thread dumps, startup timeline, GraalVM reachability-metadata generation, PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB internals, N+1 detection, Spring Security failures, Resilience4j, Spring AI, LangChain4j and Sentry-style grouped exceptions.

Dubois says there are too many panels for a human, and that the real audience is coding agents. An MCP server, an agent skill and a CLI expose the same data. In the demo, GitHub Copilot found 6 problematic transactions out of 28, and teams use the CLI to block deployment on a poor score. The upcoming V2 stores events in a graph database for change-impact analysis and run-to-run diffs, so an agent can confirm a fix worked. It runs algorithms to spot problems such as held connections or errors behind a 200 response, and adds an optional bytecode-instrumentation agent costing about 5% for code paths, network calls (it caught Liquibase calling home), files and processes.
keyPoints: Setup is one dependency in Maven or Gradle, which exposes a /bootui URL. The same engine and UI serve Spring MVC, Spring WebFlux and Quarkus through separate adapters.
Over 400 rules (architecture, Spring, Hibernate mappings, REST practices, SQL configuration, memory) report the issue, the location and the fix, which suits agents as well as humans.
Database panels go from PostgreSQL/MySQL session and index data, through Spring transactions and rollbacks, to JDBC-level SQL capture with N+1 detection, plus Flyway and Liquibase control.
An MCP server, an agent skill and a CLI expose all panels, and the CLI can be used as a CI quality gate on score, rollbacks or exception counts.
V2 adds an event graph for change-impact analysis and run-to-run diffs, and an optional bytecode agent with roughly 5% overhead that is not meant for production.
takeaways: Add the BootUI dependency to a real Spring Boot or Quarkus app in development and run the scorecard.
Turn on the BootUI MCP server or skill so your coding agent can inspect transactions, SQL and exceptions at runtime instead of guessing from source.
Use the CLI in CI to fail a build on a poor scorecard or too many rolled-back transactions.

quotes.text: The target audience, of course, is AI agents, AI coding agents, who are going to connect to your app, see all those issues, and fix them.

watchIf: You build Spring Boot or Quarkus apps and want runtime insight into transactions, SQL and exceptions that you or a coding agent can act on.
